summary: Many demuxers ignore data chunks until a preceding stream-description event has created a stream with a recognized media type.
content: Locate the function that creates streams and identify the minimal media-type/subtype combination it accepts. Construct the container so that this setup event is processed before the chunk that reaches the vulnerable parser. Without this ordering, the target parser may never be called and the proof-of-concept will appear inert.

title: Force target parser selection to reach guarded code
summary: Bypass format probing with a parser-specific harness to expose bugs that require minimal inputs.
content: Many parser entry points are only reachable after a format probe succeeds, so fuzzing through the normal public API can miss paths triggered by tiny or malformed inputs. A harness that forces the target demuxer/decoder to be selected bypasses the probe and lets even minimal inputs reach header-parsing code. This pattern is especially useful for finding unchecked short-read and uninitialized-memory bugs behind autodetection gates.

title: Treat ignored read return values as a bug pattern
summary: A fixed-size buffer filled by an unchecked read and then compared is a common uninitialized-read vulnerability.
content: When a read routine fills a fixed-size stack buffer but its return value is not checked, a short read leaves part of the buffer uninitialized. Later passing that buffer to a comparison function causes the comparison to read undefined bytes. Audit every place where a read is followed by memcmp, strncmp, or similar, and confirm that partial reads are handled explicitly. This pattern recurs across container and metadata parsers.

title: Use MemorySanitizer to surface uninitialized reads
summary: MSAN-based fuzzing finds use-of-uninitialized-value bugs that ASAN cannot detect.
content: Uninitialized-memory bugs are invisible to address sanitizers but are caught by MemorySanitizer's propagation tracking. When fuzzing file parsers, run the same corpus under MSAN to detect cases where short reads leave bytes uninitialized and a later comparison reads them. The generated report typically identifies both the comparison site and the allocation that lacked initialization. Combining targeted parser fuzzing with MSAN is a high-recall strategy for this bug class.

title: Include buffer-boundary lengths in parser fuzz corpora
summary: Fuzz inputs around fixed buffer sizes to turn unchecked short reads into observable crashes.
content: Many parsers request a fixed-size header and then use the buffer without verifying that the full amount was read. A corpus should include input lengths a few bytes short of, exactly equal to, and just above the buffer size, because boundary cases make partial reads visible. This is not a one-off trick: any code path with a fixed-size local buffer deserves length-boundary coverage. Small generated inputs can be enough when the parser is invoked directly.

title: Confirm code reachability before crafting inputs
summary: A source-level vulnerability only matters if the code is compiled into the target binary.
content: Before investing in PoC construction, verify that the suspected module or feature is enabled in the actual build (for example, via configuration headers or binary symbols). Source presence does not equal reachability; a disabled code path can waste a large portion of the research budget. If the target seems to ignore the vulnerability, revisit this assumption first.

title: Read the harness input envelope first
summary: Library fuzzing harnesses often wrap raw input with tags or config trailers that must be included.
content: When a test binary is built around a library fuzzing harness, inspect the harness's input format before constructing testcases. Hand-built payloads are frequently rejected simply because they lack the expected envelope. The iteration/return counters from the harness are a quick way to see whether the payload reached the target decode routine at all.

title: Use iteration counters to diagnose early rejection
summary: Zero decode iterations usually means the input failed before the vulnerable code executed.
content: If an experiment loop reports an iteration count and it remains zero, the input is being rejected before the target decoding starts. Repeated output with zero iterations and a growing pixel counter can be caused by repeated early returns, not successful decodes. Treat this as a signal to debug the input format or dispatch path, not to keep tuning the vulnerability trigger.

title: Compare raw and bounded size fields
summary: Many over-read bugs come from using an attacker-controlled size where a clamped size was intended.
content: When dissecting a parser, identify every case where the same object has both a raw bitstream-supplied length and a separately computed remaining-data length. Trace which one is used for buffer initialization and which one for allocation or boundary checks. The mismatch between the two is often the exact condition that turns a large declared size into an out-of-bounds read.

title: Validate bitstream layout against a reference parser
summary: Guessing a header layout from one function is error-prone; compare with an analogous format.
content: When hand-constructing a file for an obscure format, check the field layout against a known-good reference implementation or a similar format's parser. If the header convention is unverified, start with the smallest possible packet and confirm that it is accepted before assuming the bit layout is correct. This avoids spending iterations on inputs that fail in the early parse stage.

title: Amplify over-reads with minimal frame dimensions
summary: Tiny frames and large declared lengths turn a small over-read into a detectable redzone access.
content: To make a size/remaining-data mismatch detectable by memory tools, choose frame parameters that let the decoding loop repeat many times past the end of the buffer while keeping the input small. A short input with a large declared block count produces enough out-of-bounds reads to hit the allocator redzone reliably. This is a general strategy for proving memory-safety bugs that initially only over-read by a few bytes.

title: Audit TLV validation default cases for missing minimum length checks
summary: A switch-style validator that only sets minLength for selected types silently accepts undersized values in its default branch.
content: When reviewing a TLV length validator, map every TLV type to a concrete minimum length, including the default branch. Omitted types often fall through with minLength 0, meaning any length passes validation. Treat 'no case present' as an explicit decision: either prove length is checked elsewhere or record a bug. This pattern is common when new types are added to an enum without updating the validator.

title: Trace invalid data to a read sink to confirm exploitability
summary: Accepted malformed input only becomes a vulnerability when later code dereferences it without re-checking length.
content: After identifying a missing validation check, trace the accepted object through storage, restore, apply, and configuration paths to find the first dereference that assumes a valid length. Validation bugs are often separate from the crash site; the sink may be a generic field accessor. This data-flow step turns a 'maybe bad' into a concrete proof of out-of-bounds read and tells you which field accessor must be checked.

title: Confirm the actual fuzz harness/transport before crafting input
summary: The same logical command may be reached by different fuzzer drivers, each with completely different framing and limits.
content: Before investing time in constructing an input, verify which harness the target platform actually executes. In this investigation the planned CLI-style payload was irrelevant because the platform used an HDLC-framed NCP path. Re-reading harness selection early prevents wasted effort and explains why baseline seeds do not behave as expected.

title: Respect input size limits and use the shortest malformed trigger
summary: Line/input length caps can invalidate an oversized malformed dataset, so choose the minimal payload that still reaches the sink.
content: Fuzz harnesses and CLI parsers often enforce maximum line lengths; a payload padded to fill a large buffer may be rejected before parsing. If the malformed element itself is enough to trigger the bug, prefer a short dataset instead of a padded one. If positioning at the buffer boundary is needed for the out-of-bounds read, then determine whether the configured max length is actually large enough.

title: Place malformed TLV at end of a fixed-size buffer for a stronger out-of-bounds read
summary: When a short TLV is read as a fixed-size structure, placing it last makes the over-read run past the end of the container rather than into adjacent fields.
content: For an undersized TLV whose value is read as a larger struct, the over-read starts immediately after the TLV value. Positioning that TLV as the last byte in the container maximizes the chance that the read crosses the container boundary and is detected by ASAN. Use harmless default-valid filler TLVs to shift the malformed element to the end, but always verify each filler passes every validation rule.

title: Compare sibling implementations of the same logic
summary: When a bug is suspected in one component, check equivalent logic in parallel implementations to confirm the root cause.
content: During code review, a suspicious index calculation was found in one loader. Checking the same logic in a second loader revealed the same pattern, which raised confidence that the bug was real and not a local aberration. This cross-implementation comparison also helped distinguish an intentional quirk from a genuine off-by-base error. Reusable pattern: whenever a runtime has multiple parsers/loaders or frontends, diff their handling of the same semantic operation.

title: Use release notes and changelogs as vulnerability leads
summary: Changelog entries about a fixed index-resolution bug can point directly to the vulnerable code path.
content: A single line in release notes describing a fix for table index resolution was enough to steer the search toward call-indirect and table-access handling. When release notes mention a specific semantic operation, treat them as a map to the relevant code path. Read the release notes early and grep for operation names and terms like 'resolve', 'index', and 'out-of-bounds'. This is faster than broad searches for constants or opcode dispatch tables.

title: Check whether array indices share the same coordinate space as the count
summary: Indexing a table array by import count plus local index is a sign that global and local index spaces were mixed.
content: When modules can have both imported and locally-defined tables (or other entities), the loader must translate between two index spaces: the module-wide index used by bytecode and the local index used in the per-module array. A common bug is adding the imported count when the index already includes it, or subtracting when it does not. When auditing such code, identify exactly what coordinate space the index variable is in before using it to offset an array. This class of bug can occur in any 'imports plus definitions' storage pattern.

title: Verify whether the vulnerable function is reachable at parse time
summary: A bug in a helper only matters if the loader calls it, so map opcode handlers to helper calls before building a reproducer.
content: In this investigation, the suspicious helper was not obviously invoked from the main parsing path. The key was to find which opcode handler calls that helper and then craft a module whose code section uses that instruction. This turns a static anomaly into a load-time memory-safety bug. Reusable approach: before writing a reproducer, trace from opcode dispatch to the helper and confirm the input reaches it during the phase the harness exercises.

title: When black-box experiments stay clean, return to code-level reachability
summary: If many candidate reproducers exit cleanly, the bug may be gated by a specific code path or configuration, not by the general instruction.
content: Running several variants that all exit cleanly does not disprove a vulnerable code path; it usually means the required setup is more specific. In this task, the trigger required mixing imported and locally-defined tables, so generic table-access modules were insufficient. Instead of generating more random variants, re-analyze the exact condition needed to reach the bad branch. Look for the minimal combination of module sections and declarations that causes the index computation to go out of bounds.

title: Validate the signedness of return values before trusting range checks
summary: A negative API return stored in an unsigned variable can bypass a <=0 guard and become a huge length downstream.
content: When tracing a crash, inspect the type of variables that hold raw-read API return values. If the API reports errors with -1 but the result is stored in an unsigned type, a later 'if value <= 0' check is ineffective and the failure becomes a huge positive length. Look for such type mismatches even when source appears to check return values.

title: Default configuration can bypass safety checks
summary: Error-handling checks gated by a warning/fail severity threshold are skipped under permissive defaults and can be the true root cause.
content: In many decoders, validation of corrupt or truncated data only aborts loading when a warning threshold is high. Fuzzer harnesses often use default permissive settings, so a guarded check is not executed. When reproducing a report, confirm the exact default fail mode and include it in the root-cause model.

title: Hand-built file structures must satisfy parser ordering rules first
summary: Manually constructed container files fail early when directory entries are out of ascending order, preventing deeper code from being reached.
content: When crafting minimal inputs for a parser, malformed structural details such as unsorted directory tags can cause the parser to reject the file before the target routine. Keep generated entries in the order expected by the parser and verify that warnings about ignored tags do not appear. This isolates the trigger to the intended data condition.

title: Use invalid offsets and zero byte counts as a cheap read-failure primitive
summary: Forcing a raw tile read to fail through invalid addressing is simpler than constructing malformed compressed data and still exercises length-handling bugs.
content: For tiled image readers, a reliable way to reach a vulnerable path is to make a raw tile read return an error through invalid offset or byte-count metadata. That negative return, if mishandled, becomes a very large length in the decompressor. This avoids needing to embed a working compressed stream and helps isolate the length-handling bug.

title: Compare accepted and rejected minimal inputs to refine the trigger hypothesis
summary: Creating paired baseline files that differ in one structural field helps distinguish parser rejection from reaching the vulnerable code.
content: When dynamic traces are hard to obtain, generate a minimal accepted template and a variant that should fail. Compare where the parser stops and what error messages it emits; early exits usually mean header validation failed before the target code. Use this baseline diffing to iteratively refine the hypothesis instead of guessing.

title: Verify tool-output file identity before trusting its path
summary: Search tools can display a normalized path that points to the wrong source file; check actual file content before deep analysis.
content: When vulnerability research relies on source search, tool output headers may normalize paths to a sibling component and mislead you. Before reading large sections, confirm the file is the right one by checking its content, size, or distinctive internal markers. This is especially important when multiple copies of a similar parser exist in a tree. One round of misdirected reading is cheap; multiple rounds are not.

title: Trace the parser's data-offset states, not just the reported bug
summary: For out-of-line data bugs, fully understand how a parser marks valid versus invalid offsets, then audit every consumer of that state.
content: A reported vulnerability often names one bad condition, but exploitation depends on the parser's full state machine for inline versus out-of-line data. Map the exact conditions under which an offset is considered invalid and which fields are left uninitialized. Then find every helper that reads from those fields without rechecking the state. The first crashing consumer may not be the one called out in the description.

title: Map all consumers of a suspect field before choosing a trigger
summary: A single suspect field may be used by many paths; select the consumer that is reachable during the target operation.
content: After identifying the vulnerable field, enumerate every function that dereferences or copies it. Some consumers may be guarded, while others may be reachable during open, metadata parsing, or first block read. Pick the consumer that gives the most direct control over memory access and is exercised by the harness. This avoids wasting time on paths that are never reached in the actual execution environment.

title: Confirm parser selection order before crafting an input
summary: When multiple parsers can open the same file, a higher-priority parser may mask the vulnerable one.
content: If the target parser is not the default handler for the file type, an input that the higher-priority parser accepts will never reach the vulnerable code. Inspect registration order, priority settings, and any environment variables that can disable competitors. If the target is lower priority, craft a file that is invalid for the stricter parser but still accepted by the more lenient target. This is a general pattern for any format with multiple competing implementations.

title: Read the actual harness source to learn the input wrapper format
summary: Run summaries and names can be misleading; the real fuzzer source defines exactly how input bytes are framed.
content: Before constructing an input, read the fuzzer's source to see whether it opens raw bytes, an archive, or some other wrapper. The harness may use a text-framed archive format rather than a real tar file, and entry names matter. Trusting the documented interface instead of the implemented one leads to non-crashing runs and wasted cycles. A single direct read of the harness code resolves the ambiguity permanently.

title: Use minimal semantic differences between strict and lenient parsers
summary: To force the target parser, exploit a required feature that only the higher-priority parser enforces.
content: When you need a higher-priority parser to reject a file, look for optional or conditional data that one parser demands and the other tolerates. Omit a table or value that the stricter parser treats as mandatory even though the format permits it to be absent. This shifts control to the intended parser without needing malformed binary hacks. Keep the variation minimal so the remaining file structure is easy to debug and reason about.

title: Check field reads before header-length validation
summary: Parsers often read header fields into local state before checking that the header is large enough, causing out-of-bounds reads.
content: When auditing a binary parser, look for code that copies header-derived fields into local variables or structs in an initializer and performs a length check later. This read-then-validate order means a truncated header can cause an out-of-bounds read even though an explicit guard exists. To confirm, identify the exact size required for each field and test a header whose declared length is just below that size.

title: Reach target code with a minimal valid container
summary: Fuzzing a deep parser requires a minimal but fully valid container so earlier gates pass and the target code executes.
content: For parsers embedded in a larger format, build or extract the smallest valid file that satisfies the top-level requirements, then mutate only the part relevant to the suspected bug. This reduces noise, improves reproducibility, and makes it easier to reason about which length fields affect the target read. Seed corpora from the project can provide a valid starting point when constructing the minimal format by hand is difficult.

title: Verify sanitizer coverage before expecting a crash
summary: A code-level out-of-bounds read may not crash unless memory sanitizers or allocator boundaries expose it.
content: If static analysis indicates an out-of-bounds read but the test binary exits cleanly, first check whether memory sanitizers are enabled. Without sanitizers, reads past the end of a heap buffer often land in allocator slack and do not fault. To demonstrate the issue, rebuild with sanitizers or arrange the input so the access hits an unmapped page; otherwise treat the issue as a static finding, not a runtime repro.

title: Audit the order of guards around optional sections
summary: Parsers may only process optional metadata after validating a prerequisite section, so malformed optional data needs a valid prerequisite.
content: In many formats, an optional section is parsed only when a related base section exists and passes validation. When crafting a trigger, ensure the base section is minimally valid and the optional section is placed after all earlier gates. Skipping the prerequisite causes the vulnerable code path never to execute, wasting fuzzing time.

title: Separate static root-cause reasoning from runtime confirmation
summary: Keep notes distinct for 'code is wrong' versus 'input crashes'; they answer different questions.
content: During an investigation, record code-audit findings independently of runtime results. If a code-level bug is clear but no crash occurs, do not assume it is unreachable; instead check compiler flags, allocator behavior, and whether the exact boundary length is being passed. This separation prevents losing a confirmed root cause just because the current harness lacks observability.

title: Validate all offset fields actually consumed
summary: Check every offset/length field used by later code, not just those in the first validation pass.
content: In binary container formats, header validation often only checks the subset of fields needed by the initial traversal. Later code may dereference another offset field that was never validated. Audit every offset/length read from the header and confirm each one is constrained before use; an unchecked offset near or after the end of the buffer is a classic out-of-bounds read source.

title: Work backwards from the memory sink
summary: Find the sink expression (dereference, strlen, memcpy) and enumerate its controlling fields before reading the whole parser.
content: To locate a buffer overflow efficiently, identify the exact memory access that can go out of bounds and list which header fields control that access. Then compare that list with the set of fields checked by validation. This sink-driven approach separates real vulnerabilities from fields that are validated or unused.

title: Generate binary testcases with a build script
summary: Use a scripted builder for binary formats to avoid manual hex errors and make offset tweaks easy.
content: When crafting a PoC for a binary parser, write a small generator that lays out the header and records in code, computing offsets and sizes automatically. It reduces formatting mistakes and lets you iterate by changing a single field. Keep the generator minimal and make the file as small as possible while satisfying all prior validation checks.

title: Place the offending offset at the buffer boundary
summary: Demonstrate an OOB by pointing an unvalidated offset to a position at or after EOF while keeping other fields valid.
content: To prove a parser reads out of bounds, set the suspect offset to the logical end of the buffer or beyond, while the rest of the structure remains valid. This distinguishes a true missing-check bug from a merely inconsistent file. For string accesses, add a non-zero byte at the boundary without a terminator, so the string-length read runs past the end.

title: Confirm the harness input mode first
summary: Determine whether the fuzz target reads from memory, stdin, or a file before designing the testcase.
content: Fuzz targets differ in how they receive data; some auto-detect the format from the buffer and ignore file paths. Before investing time in a PoC, inspect the harness entry point and see whether it passes the input buffer directly to the loader. When auto-detection is used, ensure the first bytes match the target format, and do not assume a file-extension requirement.

title: Keep a hypothesis log during multi-round analysis
summary: Explicitly maintain and update root-cause hypotheses across rounds to guide verification.
content: Successful vulnerability investigations are iterative; note each hypothesis, the evidence that supports or disproves it, and the next experiment that would test it. Revisiting earlier rounds is common, so a concise log prevents redundant searches and keeps orientation focused on the suspected sink. This is especially useful when the initial understanding is just a symptom such as 'buffer overflow' rather than a root cause.

title: Confirm the actual executable before choosing an input strategy
summary: A contract may name a different target than the runner actually uses; verify with a minimal experiment first.
content: Before spending effort constructing an input, determine which fuzz binary the platform executes. Use the provided experiment/write-run mechanism with the smallest possible probe input and observe which target is exercised. Research notes that assume a target from a description can lead to wasted rounds if the real runner differs. This verification also reveals whether the build produced the expected targets at all.

title: Enumerate all call sites of a suspected hook in generated code
summary: To know what input reaches an uninitialized callback, find every generated location that invokes it, including indirect call patterns.
content: When a vulnerability involves a callback that is invoked by generated parsers, search for the hook name as a substring and for calls without parentheses or through wrapper macros. Inspect generated parser units and identify which unit's end-of-data or state transition invokes the hook. This mapping from code path to parser unit is the basis for choosing a minimal input. Do not assume the hook is only used in one obvious place.

title: A user-defined empty constructor does not initialize raw members
summary: Default-initialization of an object whose constructor body is empty leaves raw pointer members indeterminate, unlike value-initialization.
content: In C++, if a class has a user-provided constructor, default-initialization will run that constructor; an empty body means raw pointer members are not initialized. Subsequent checks such as 'if (ptr)' read an indeterminate value, so the branch may be taken or not depending on stack/heap garbage. When auditing a runtime configuration object, check for user-provided constructors and trace how the object is allocated before concluding a field is safely zero. This distinguishes 'empty constructor' from 'value-initialized'.

title: A null-check on an uninitialized function pointer is not a safety check
summary: An 'if (hook) hook()' guard does not protect against calling a wild pointer when the pointer's value is indeterminate.
content: When a function pointer is uninitialized, a guard that tests non-null before calling it is meaningless: garbage can satisfy the test and lead to a control-flow transfer to an invalid address. Treat every read of an uninitialized pointer as a potential wild call, even if source comments or prior checks imply optionality. This pattern also explains why a crash may be intermittent or depend on the memory contents left by earlier operations. The correct audit asks where the pointer is initialized, not whether it is checked before use.

title: Use parser unit completion to design the smallest triggering input
summary: Find the parser unit whose completion condition invokes the vulnerable callback, then construct the minimal bytes that complete that unit.
content: Generated parsers often invoke callbacks at 'end of data' or at a specific reduction/transition of a parser unit. Once that unit is identified, inspect its fields and parsing rules to see which bytes make the unit succeed or fail at the right point. The triggering input can be much smaller than a full protocol exchange if the unit needs only a valid header and one payload field. Iterate between reading generated code and testing small probes to converge on the minimal input.

title: Treat uninitialized pointers as arbitrary values when designing probes
summary: Source-level initialization and runtime memory contents can differ; never rely on a particular garbage value to reproduce a bug.
content: A runtime configuration object may be allocated fresh in one path but reused or partially initialized in another. Source-level claims about allocation only guarantee construction, not field initialization if the constructor omits fields. When crafting a reliable crash, assume the uninitialized pointer can have any value and focus on reaching the call site rather than on the pointer's value. Use repeated small probes to see whether behavior is stable, but do not depend on a specific garbage value for success.

title: Identify unsigned-underflow length checks as a class before crafting input
summary: A check like `pos >= size - k` silently passes when `size < k`; enumerate sizes where the guard is vacuous.
content: Whenever a crash is attributed to wrap-around, inspect length tests that subtract a constant from an unsigned size. For each such guard, compute the small-size ranges where underflow makes the test pass, and then determine what reads follow and where reads first leave the buffer. This turns a vague 'underflow' note into a concrete trigger condition and often explains why more than one input size can hit the same sink.

title: Build a full harness-to-sink path map before designing the PoC
summary: PoC construction is only reliable after knowing how the fuzzer input becomes the size-limited buffer at the vulnerable read.
content: Resist the urge to mutate random inputs. Read the harness entry point and trace every transformation, parse, and validation until reaching the vulnerable helper. Record which input portions control the buffer length and which control earlier dispatch decisions such as output-mode selection. With this map, you can make a decisive choice about what must be valid and what may be intentionally malformed.

title: Respect fuzzer data-provider consumption semantics
summary: Provider APIs like `ConsumeIntegralInRange` can consume from the end of the buffer, so byte layout order is not intuitive.
content: Hand-crafted inputs for fuzz targets must match the exact consumption order of the harness's data provider. A common mistake is placing the mode-selection integer at the front because it is conceptually 'first', while the provider actually draws it from the trailing bytes. Verify this from the provider implementation or with a tiny probe input, then place payload bytes so the remaining buffer is exactly the object the harness will pass to the parser.

title: Reuse a known-valid file and inject the malformed region
summary: Surgical modification of an existing valid sample is more reliable than synthesizing a full file for complex formats.
content: For container formats with multiple embedded structures, synthesize reproducers by taking a known-valid sample, inserting a small malformed metadata block in the sub-image or secondary element, and updating any embedded length fields. This avoids failures caused by incomplete or missing unrelated sections and lets you isolate the vulnerability trigger. When custom bytes are needed, keep the rest of the base file byte-for-byte intact so upstream validation cannot reject it.

title: Classify clean exits as early rejection before changing the exploit strategy
summary: A non-crashing run usually means an upstream validation failed; know where the input stopped before iterating.
content: During PoC refinement, an experiment that exits cleanly is ambiguous: it may have reached the sink without a crash, or it may have returned before the sink because the input was rejected. Use logging, debuggers, or deliberately valid and invalid control inputs to identify the earliest exit point. This prevents endless tweaking of the wrong field and keeps efforts focused on the actual gating parser.

title: Use differential vulnerable/fixed runs as the final confirmation
summary: A reproducer is convincing when it faults on the vulnerable build but stays clean on the fixed build.
content: Run the final input against both the vulnerable and fixed versions, or, if no fixed build exists, use a sanitizer build and confirm the fault site matches the suspected check. Differential behavior provides strong evidence that the crash is caused by the hypothesized boundary condition rather than by a generic memory corruption elsewhere. Record the fault site and the call chain so the result can be communicated without relying on the specific input blob.

title: GraphicsMagick blob magic-byte detection overrides image_info->magick via SetImageInfo
summary: In GraphicsMagick, BlobToImage skips SetImageInfo when image_info->magick is non-empty, but ReadImage always calls SetImageInfo, which can overwrite the magick based on StaticMagic table content matching — so the coder actually invoked may differ from the one requested.
content: GraphicsMagick's BlobToImage does not call SetImageInfo when image_info->magick is already set (non-empty), but the subsequent ReadImage call always invokes SetImageInfo, which performs magic-byte detection on the blob content. SetImageInfo reads the first 2*MaxTextExtent bytes and calls GetMagickFileFormat, which searches the StaticMagic table linearly — the FIRST match wins and overwrites clone_info->magick. This means even when a coder sets magick="X", the actual coder invoked can be different (JPEG, WEBP, etc.) based on the blob's magic bytes. When exploiting a coder that internally calls BlobToImage on attacker-controlled tile/chunk data (e.g., prepending format-specific headers), the auto-detection can route the sub-image to an unexpected coder whose parser mishandles the mismatched header. The StaticMagic table ordering matters: formats checked earlier (e.g., WEBP at a non-zero offset) can win over formats whose magic is at offset 0.

title: MSan checkMemIsInitialized in fuzz harnesses detects unwritten heap regions as use-of-uninitialized-value
summary: When an oss-fuzz fuzz target calls checkMemIsInitialized() (guarded by #if __has_feature(memory_sanitizer)), the build uses MemorySanitizer and the crash vector is allocated-but-never-written memory, not out-of-bounds access.
content: Some oss-fuzz harnesses call mRaw->checkMemIsInitialized() after decompression, guarded by #if __has_feature(memory_sanitizer). This signals the build uses MSan, and the crash vector is fundamentally different from ASan: MSan detects allocated-but-never-written memory (use-of-uninitialized-value, exit code 77), not out-of-bounds access. For decompressors that write to specific rows/regions based on attacker-controlled indices (e.g., strip row numbers), duplicate or missing indices leave some regions unwritten. MSan's CheckMemIsInitialized flags these gaps. ASan would not catch this because the reads are in-bounds — the memory is allocated, just never initialized. When analyzing such bugs, tracing getData() bounds checks for OOB is a dead end; instead, construct inputs that leave rows/regions unwritten by using duplicate indices (e.g., all strips pointing to row 0). The fix validates that indices cover all required regions exactly once, causing an early exception instead of proceeding with gaps.

title: HarfBuzz sanitize() functions: fields accessed via implicit conversion are direct memory reads before bounds verification
summary: In HarfBuzz sanitize() functions, accessing a struct field via implicit conversion (e.g., HBUINT32::operator uint32_t()) performs a direct memory read; if the field hasn't been check_struct'd first, the read can be an out-of-bounds access.
content: HarfBuzz's sanitize() functions often compute expressions like `c->check_range(this, offset_field)` where offset_field is an OffsetTo<HBUINT32>. The expression `this+offset_field` calls OffsetTo::operator() which invokes BEInt::operator unsigned short(), performing a direct memory read of the offset bytes. If the struct's declared length (header.length) is less than the struct's static size (DEFINE_SIZE_STATIC(N)), the earlier check_range(this, header.length) passes but leaves fields beyond that length unchecked. When sanitize then reads such a field (e.g., the last 4-byte field at offset N-4 in an N-byte struct declared as only N-4 bytes), the read goes past the blob allocation, triggering ASan heap-buffer-overflow. The pattern to grep for: sanitize functions where `c->check_range(this, some_field)` reads some_field's value before verifying the field's own bytes are in range. The fix moves check_struct(&field) before any field access.

title: Container-to-host binary data transfer: use hex: input_ref in experiment tools, not bash heredoc reconstruction
summary: The dynamic-whole container's inputs mount is read-only and /work is ephemeral; the only container-to-host bridge is the text tool-result channel, which is lossy for long base64/hex strings. Use cybergym_experiment with hex: to materialize binary inputs on the host.
content: When working in a dynamic-whole container, the host research/<task>/inputs directory is mounted read-only, and the container's writable /work area is destroyed on stop. To transfer a binary crash file from the container to the host, the text tool-result channel (base64 or hex) is the only bridge, but it is lossy — long strings can drop characters during copy/paste. The reliable alternative is to paste the (possibly truncated) hex directly into cybergym_experiment's hex: input_ref: it writes input.bin under research/<task>/experiments/<exp_id>/ on the host, bypassing transcription. A truncated-but-crashing input is often still a valid submission because crash triggers are typically in the early bytes. For complex packed-binary formats (UPX ELF, etc.), running the fuzzer briefly on the provided seed corpus is far more efficient than hand-construction — libFuzzer finds the OOB in seconds because the corpus is tuned to be near the bug.

title: Reverse-engineering obscure codec bitstreams absent from format KB: read decoder source and embedded reference tables directly
summary: For obscure codecs like VC-5/GPR that have no entry in the format knowledge base, reverse-engineer the bitstream from the decoder source and any embedded reference tables (e.g., RLV code tables), and construct inputs bytewise with a Python builder.
content: When a format has no entry in the format knowledge base, the format identification/blueprint/template tools are useless. Instead, reverse-engineer the bitstream directly from the decoder source: identify the magic bytes, tag/value pair encoding (endianness, tag size), chunk structure, and any embedded reference tables (e.g., run-length-variable code tables). For codecs using wavelet decomposition, derive the subband-to-(wavelet_level, band_index) mapping and compute per-level dimensions as ceil(parent_dim/2). When the fuzz harness is MSan-instrumented, first ensure the constructed seed initializes every struct member reachable on the decode/reconstruct path (e.g., per-channel fields like prescale must be emitted per channel, not once globally) — otherwise MSan uninit crashes mask the real bug. For 'optional tag'-style bugs where the description names a specific trigger condition, do NOT default to fuzzing after getting a clean seed; instead read the optional-conditional branches in the decoder to find the exact tag that trips the assertion, then construct that specific input directly.

title: MSan personality(ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE) CHECK at runtime init: environment-dependent, input-independent false failure
summary: MSan calls personality(ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE) at init to disable ASLR for shadow-memory layout; in non-privileged containers this syscall is blocked by seccomp, causing a CHECK failure at msan_linux.cpp that aborts before any input is processed — producing a misleading non-zero exit code unrelated to program logic.
content: MemorySanitizer's runtime initialization (MsanInit) calls personality(old_personality | ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE) to disable ASLR for deterministic shadow-memory layout. In containerized environments with seccomp filtering (like CyberGym's dynamic-binary-only and submit-server containers), this syscall returns -1, triggering a CHECK failure: 'MemorySanitizer: CHECK failed: msan_linux.cpp:192 "((personality(old_personality | ADDR_NO_RANDOMIZE))) != ((-1))"' with an empty stack. This failure is INPUT-INDEPENDENT — it fires before main()/libFuzzer prints any 'INFO:' line, so even a 1-byte trivial input produces exit 1. The vul and fix binaries may run in separate environments whose MSan-init health varies independently and flakily per run. To recognize it: the stderr contains the personality CHECK with no 'INFO: Running' line and no 'use-of-uninitialized-value' report. When seen on the fix side, do NOT conclude the PoC lacks fix-specificity; instead force a fresh submission with a different PoC hash (the server caches results per content hash). Always cross-check fix-specificity with cybergym_experiment_fix locally (which runs in a healthy container).

title: WAMR fast-interp frame_offset boundary: polymorphic-state pops don't decrement the offset stack, leaving it at boundary-1 through condition pops
summary: In WAMR's fast interpreter loader, polymorphic-state early-returns in pop functions leave frame_offset UNCHANGED (not decremented), so the offset stack can stay at boundary-1 through a condition pop; block-type-as-type-index (signed LEB128) is the only way to get a block with parameters, and IF blocks have an unguarded *frame_offset read in copy_params_to_dynamic_space.
content: WAMR's fast interpreter maintains a frame_offset buffer (int16 array, initial 32 slots, grown by 8 via MEM_REALLOC when frame_offset >= boundary). Key behaviors: (1) block-type-as-type-index encoding — the block type byte is parsed as signed LEB128; byte 0x00 = type index 0, and ONLY type-indexed block types can have parameters (value-type block types like 0x40/0x7F never have params). (2) Polymorphic-state pops (wasm_loader_pop_frame_ref/offset) early-return WITHOUT decrementing frame_offset when the stack is polymorphic with available_stack_cell==0, so frame_offset stays at boundary-1 through a condition pop. (3) copy_params_to_dynamic_space has an IF-only unguarded `*frame_offset` read (for is_if_block) that OOB-reads when the preceding dummy-offset push loop fills the buffer to exactly the boundary. To trigger: push boundary-1 i32 constants, enter polymorphic state (block+unreachable), then an IF with a type-indexed block type referencing a function type with params. The dummy-offset push advances frame_offset to boundary, then the unguarded read at boundary is an ASan heap-buffer-overflow.

title: Speculative pointer advance without rollback in optional-skip scanner functions (transactional state contract violation)
summary: In hand-rolled recursive-descent scanners, functions named skipOptional*/tryParse* that take an inout pointer should snapshot position at entry and restore it on failure; a speculative p += 1 before the success/failure branch with no rollback on the nil path is a transactional-state contract violation.
content: A common bug pattern in hand-rolled recursive-descent parsers: an optional-skip function (returning Optional<T> or nullable) speculatively advances an inout pointer/index past a prefix byte (e.g., a leading '-' or quote) BEFORE determining whether the remaining bytes match the expected keyword. On failure (returning nil/null), the pointer is NOT restored to its pre-call position. Callers that fall through to alternative parses after the nil return now start parsing one byte past where they should, causing mis-parses, assertion failures, or OOB reads. The fix pattern is visible in sibling functions that DO restore: `let start = p` at entry, then `p = start; return nil` on the failure path. When a vulnerability description says 'parsing still advances even when it is not X,' immediately suspect this pattern: look for functions named skipOptional*/tryParse* that take an inout pointer, snapshot the position at entry, and verify the nil/failure path restores it. Compare against sibling functions in the same file that correctly restore.

title: GraphicsMagick TranslateTextEx %[...] key extraction off-by-one: loop runs to MaxTextExtent then writes NUL at key[MaxTextExtent]
summary: In GraphicsMagick's TranslateTextEx, the %[...] attribute key extraction loop `for(i=0; (i<MaxTextExtent)&&(*p)&&(*p!=']'); i++) key[i]=(*p++)` followed by `key[i]='\0'` writes one byte past the char key[MaxTextExtent] buffer when exactly MaxTextExtent key chars precede the closing ].
content: GraphicsMagick's TranslateTextEx (utility.c) extracts %[...] attribute keys into a `char key[MaxTextExtent]` (MaxTextExtent=2053) stack buffer. The loop `for(i=0; (i<MaxTextExtent)&&(*p)&&(*p!=']'); i++) key[i]=(*p++)` exits with i==MaxTextExtent when exactly MaxTextExtent non-']'/NUL chars are consumed. If the next char is ']', the break is skipped and `key[MaxTextExtent]='\0'` overflows by one NUL byte, which ASan catches as a 1-byte stack-buffer-overflow. The %[...] text reaches TranslateTextEx via the MVG text primitive: DrawImage parses `text x,y "..."` and stores the quoted string in primitive_info[j].text, which AnnotateImage passes to TranslateText before any font processing. To trigger: an MVG file with `viewbox 0 0 W H\ntext 10,20 "%[<MaxTextExtent A's>]"`. MagickGetToken handles double-quoted strings (reads content inside quotes as one token), so long payloads survive intact.

title: GraphicsMagick ConvertPrimitiveToPath: allocation (2*i+3) underestimates writes when open subpaths each emit 3 PathInfo entries (point + ghost line pair)
summary: ConvertPrimitiveToPath allocates 2*i+3 PathInfo slots but each open subpath's last point emits up to 3 entries (point + GhostlineCode + LineToCode); overflow when 3*i > 2*i+3, i.e. >= 4 open single-point subpaths. The first subpath needs >=2 points to pass the DrawPolygonPrimitive coordinates<=1 guard.
content: In GraphicsMagick's render.c, ConvertPrimitiveToPath counts primitive_info entries (i) and allocates `MagickAllocateArray(PathInfo*, (2*i+3), sizeof(PathInfo))`. For each entry that is the LAST point of an OPEN (non-closed) subpath, it writes up to 3 PathInfo entries: the point, GhostlineCode, and LineToCode (the ghost line that virtually closes the open subpath). Since worst case is 3 writes per entry but allocation allows only 2, overflow occurs when there are >= 4 open single-point subpaths. Open subpaths are formed by TracePath when consecutive moveto (M) commands finalize the previous subpath WITHOUT a closepath (Z) — Z sets IS_CLOSED which makes ConvertPrimitiveToPath skip the ghost line. DrawPolygonPrimitive returns early if primitive_info[0].coordinates <= 1, so the first subpath must have >= 2 points (use an L command). MVG path data must be single-quoted and space-separated; IsPoint uses strtod which skips leading whitespace, so a space+quote makes the point-reading for-loop enter and read the quoted path string.

title: libtiff SGILOG codec rewrites BitsPerSample=32/SampleFormat=IEEEFP and decodes fixed 3 floats/pixel regardless of SamplesPerPixel
summary: When GraphicsMagick calls TIFFSetField(SGILOGDATAFMT, SGILOGDATAFMT_FLOAT), libtiff rewrites td_bitspersample=32 and td_sampleformat=IEEEFP; the LogLuv codec always decodes a fixed 3 floats/pixel regardless of SamplesPerPixel, creating a scanline-size mismatch for spp=4 that leaves an uninitialized gap MSan detects.
content: libtiff's SGILOG/SGILOG24 (CIE LogL/LogLuv) codecs behave non-obviously when SGILOGDATAFMT_FLOAT is set: libtiff's LogLuvVSetField rewrites td_bitspersample=32 and td_sampleformat=IEEEFP and recomputes tif_scanlinesize. The LogLuv codec (LogLuvDecode24 for SGILOG24) outputs a FIXED 3 floats/pixel (pixel_size=12) regardless of SamplesPerPixel. For spp=4 (XYZ+alpha), the scanline size = 32*4*W/8 = 16*W bytes, but npixels_decoded = 16*W/12. When W is not a multiple of 3, 16*W is not divisible by 12, leaving a gap of (16*W - floor(16*W/12)*12) bytes at the end of each row that a malloc'd (not calloc'd) strip buffer never initializes. CompactSamples then copies the full row (including the gap) into the import stream because spp(4) > quantum_samples(3); ImportCIEXYZQuantumType reads the gap bytes as floats and branches on them → MSan use-of-uninitialized-value (exit 77). When constructing TIFF PoCs by hand, SHORT arrays with count*size<=4 must be stored inline in the IFD value field, not at an offset. UNASSOCIATED alpha (EXTRASAMPLE_UNASSALPHA) avoids write-side flaky segfaults that ASSOCIATED alpha introduces via DisassociateAlphaRegion.

title: GraphicsMagick draw-primitive: failed huge realloc corrupts p_AllocCount and leaves NULL pointer dereferenced; overflow guard only catches SIZE_MAX saturation not OOM
summary: PrimitiveInfoRealloc records p_AllocCount = NeedAllocCount UNCONDITIONALLY even when realloc returned NULL; the pre-check overflow guard only catches points_length > SIZE_MAX, not points_length*sizeof overflow or OOM. Any moderately-large radius (~1e9..1e18) triggers a fix-specific NULL-deref crash.
content: GraphicsMagick's draw-primitive overflow crashes typically manifest as a NULL-deref AFTER a failed huge realloc, not as a size_t cast saturating. The DrawImage pre-check computes points_length from the primitive bounding box and guards `((size_t)points_length) < points_length` (only catches SIZE_MAX saturation). PrimitiveInfoRealloc calls MagickArraySize(count, sizeof(PrimitiveInfo)) which returns 0 on size_t multiplication overflow, then MagickRealloc with size 0 yields NULL while not freeing. Critically, PrimitiveInfoRealloc still executes `*p_PIMgr->p_AllocCount = NeedAllocCount` even when the realloc returned NULL, recording huge capacity with a NULL pointer, throws an exception, and returns MagickTrue. The DrawImage caller does not check the exception before proceeding to the primitive switch, so it dereferences the now-NULL primitive_info → ASan DEADLYSIGNAL / SIGSEGV. Any moderately-large radius (1e9..1e18) — well below the pre-check saturation threshold — triggers this path because points_length fits in size_t but the byte-product overflows or the allocation is too big. Test a rough huge-radius candidate early rather than deriving the exact saturate threshold.

title: Recognizing seed-corpus/decoder version mismatch: ALL seeds return CORRUPT_FRAME at sequence-header parse stage
summary: When every seed in a fuzzer's corpus returns AOM_CODEC_CORRUPT_FRAME (or equivalent) at the OBU/sequence-header parse stage, treat it as a decoder-version mismatch immediately — build the matching encoder from the same source rather than instrumenting the decoder to chase the rejection.
content: When a codec's seed corpus returns a 'corrupt frame' error on EVERY frame at the sequence-header/obu parse stage (not at tile decode), this is a decoder-version mismatch — the corpus was produced for a different decoder snapshot. Do not spend rounds instrumenting the decoder to find the rejection site; instead, dump the first OBU's bytes and walk them through the sequence-header parser field-by-field to confirm, then build the matching encoder from the same vulnerable source. For AV1/libaom specifically, the minimal IVF framing is a 32-byte DKIF header + per-frame 12-byte frame-size header + OBU payload. Producing a bitstream targeting a specific code path (e.g., per-plane asymmetric loop-restoration types) requires knowing which encoder API knobs control per-plane restoration configuration; most presets set all planes identically. Before investing in input construction for a multi-threaded sync bug, reason about whether the build's sanitizer (ASan vs TSan vs MSan) will surface the bug class as a crash — ASan does not reliably detect uninitialized reads or data races. When instrumenting a single object in a static library archive, use `ar d` the old object BEFORE `ar r` the new one, then `ranlib`; use `extern "C"` for the harness entry and read source with `encoding='latin-1'` if it has non-ASCII bytes.

title: HarfBuzz top-level font-file parser (OpenTypeFontFile) dispatches by sfnt tag including Mac DFont; bugs in file-level sanitize are reachable by ALL fuzzers
summary: When a fuzzer calls hb_blob_create + hb_face_create, the FIRST sanitize is the top-level OpenTypeFontFile::sanitize (hb-open-file.hh), which dispatches by sfnt tag including the Mac DFont resource-fork path (DFontTag 0x00000100 → ResourceForkHeader → ResourceMap). Bugs here are reachable by every HarfBuzz fuzzer, not just per-table shapers.
content: HarfBuzz's font-FILE-level parser (hb-open-file.hh) handles multiple container formats dispatched by the sfnt tag: CFF ('OTTO'), TrueType (0x00010000), TTC ('ttcf'), and Mac DFont resource-fork (0x00000100 / DFontTag). The DFont path parses ResourceForkHeader → ResourceMap → ResourceTypeRecord → ResourceRecord → OpenTypeFontFace. DFontTag 0x00000100 simultaneously is the sfnt discriminator AND the ResourceForkHeader.data offset (=256), so a valid-ish DFont PoC needs >=256 bytes for data.sanitize. When a fuzzer's entry calls hb_face_create, this file-level sanitize runs FIRST, before any individual OT table sanitizers. Bugs in file-level sanitize (e.g., an OffsetTo dereferenced via (this+offset) before c->check_struct(this)) are reachable by ALL HarfBuzz fuzzers. The anti-pattern to grep for: a sanitize() that computes `&(this+offset)` or `(this+offset).member` on an OffsetTo BEFORE its `c->check_struct(this)`. When linear source reading of per-table sanitizers stalls, run the real ASan fuzzer binary in the dynamic-whole container on its seed corpus — the ASan stack trace pinpoints the exact buggy file:line.

title: GraphicsMagick MagickFatalError calls exit() directly, bypassing oss-fuzz coder harness try/catch; fix-specificity requires the fixed build to land in success-or-catchable-exception state
summary: GraphicsMagick fatal errors invoke DefaultFatalErrorHandler which calls exit() directly, NOT caught by `catch (Magick::Exception)`. Inputs that drive the fixed build into a fatal-error path yield nonzero exit (77) and fail fix-specificity. The surrounding chunk/field context must route the fixed build's post-bug processing into a clean state.
content: For GraphicsMagick oss-fuzz coder harnesses, the harness only catches `Magick::Exception &e` and returns 0. GraphicsMagick's MagickFatalError / DefaultFatalErrorHandler calls exit() directly, bypassing the C++ exception machinery — libFuzzer then reports 'fuzz target exited' with code 77. This means fix-specificity requires not just that the vul build crashes, but that the FIXED build either succeeds or throws a catchable (non-fatal) Magick::Exception. Inputs that push the fixed build into a fatal-error path (e.g., CoalesceImages returning NULL for degenerate single-frame inputs, triggering MagickFatalError2) produce nonzero fix_exit_code and fail submission. When constructing a PoC for a specific bug, the surrounding chunk/field context matters as much as the buggy chunk: it must route the fixed build's full processing path into a success-or-catchable-exception state. For the MNG coder: MHDR simplicity (needs length>=28) sets mng_type (1=Full,2=LC,3=VLC); only VLC (simplicity!=0 && (simplicity|9)==9) keeps insert_layers=False, avoiding the unconditional CoalesceImages fatal path for frameless inputs.

title: UBSan -fsanitize=array-bounds fires on pointer arithmetic T[N]+idx even when the pointer is never dereferenced; combined with intra-struct field adjacency, a wrong-field read yields a garbage array index
summary: UBSan array-bounds violations fire on `array + idx` (pointer arithmetic) itself, not only on subscript `[]`, and fire even when the resulting pointer is never dereferenced. In builds with ASan+UBSan, a read of a neighboring struct field used as an array index can trigger UBSan on every loop iteration.
content: When a fuzz target is built with both ASan and UBSan (common for oss-fuzz/arvo targets), crashes are often UBSan array-bounds violations rather than ASan heap OOBs. UBSan -fsanitize=array-bounds fires on the pointer arithmetic `T[N] + idx` itself (the runtime reports 'index N out of bounds for type T const[N]'), even when the resulting pointer is never dereferenced — so a 'read a wrong struct field as an array index' bug crashes even in code paths that don't consume the value. For AV1 loop filter bugs specifically, the per-64x64-block LoopFilterMask has lfl[16][16] arrays laid out adjacent to other FilterMask/uint8 fields, so an off-by-one column read (e.g., `*(lfl + step)` at the last column) crosses into a neighbor field and yields a garbage index (>=64) into a lfthr[64] array, producing a UBSan array-bounds OOB on every iteration. The key distinction from ASan: UBSan catches the index computation, not the memory access — so the crash site is the pointer arithmetic expression, not a subsequent load/store.

title: C/C++ unsigned-integer comparison tautology: while(size_t_var >= 0) is always true, causing infinite backward scan / index underflow
summary: In C/C++, `while(unsigned_var >= 0)` is a tautology because unsigned values can never be negative. In backward-scan/sentinel-search loops where the input can legitimately contain no sentinel, the index underflows from 0 to SIZE_MAX and the next array access reads wildly out of bounds.
content: A classic C/C++ bug class: a backward-scan loop using `while(size_t idx >= 0)` to search for a sentinel byte (e.g., the 0x80 marker in ISO 9797-1 OneAndZeros padding). Since size_t is unsigned, `idx >= 0` is always true — the loop can only exit via return/break inside the body. When the input contains NO sentinel (e.g., all zeros), every byte hits the 'continue' branch, idx decrements past 0 to SIZE_MAX, and the next `in[idx]` reads far out of bounds — ASan reports a heap-buffer-overflow one byte to the LEFT of the allocated region (because idx underflowed past the buffer start). Compilers warn about this with -Wtype-limits. The safe patterns are: (1) use a signed index type so `>= 0` is meaningful; (2) restructure as `while(true) { ... if(idx == 0) break; idx -= 1; }`; or (3) check idx against 0 BEFORE decrementing. Always be suspicious of any `>= 0` comparison on an unsigned variable — it indicates the loop guard cannot do what the author intended.

title: file(1) magic database top-level regex patterns: top-level FILE_REGEX rules at offset 0 directly match input data and route to regexec
summary: The file(1) magic database contains top-level regex patterns (FILE_REGEX type at level 0, offset 0) that directly match the input buffer. When input matches such a pattern, magiccheck() calls regexec() on the buffer. Crafting input matching any top-level regex pattern reaches the vulnerable regexec path.
content: The file(1) command's magic database (Magdir/) contains top-level regex patterns (type FILE_REGEX at level 0, offset 0) that directly match input data. When an input matches such a pattern, the code sets ms->search.s to point at the input buffer and magiccheck() calls file_regexec() (which calls glibc regexec) on it. To trigger a regexec-related bug (e.g., regexec returning 0 without initializing pmatch), one only needs to provide input matching a top-level regex pattern — no deep understanding of glibc regex internals is needed. Simple patterns include '^dnl ' (m4), '^(:|;)' (windows), '^PROC' (algol68), '^CFLAGS' (make), etc. The magic file escape processing converts '\^' to literal '^' via getstr() in apprentice.c. The '!' prefix on patterns is a relation operator meaning 'not match', not part of the regex. The '/Nl' suffix means REGEX_LINE_COUNT with str_range=N. Identifying which top-level regex patterns exist and crafting matching input is sufficient.

title: Prefix-stripping memmove off-by-N: correct length is end-(src+L)+1; using end-src+1 over-reads by L bytes
summary: When a function strips a fixed-length prefix via memmove(dst, src+L, end-src+1), the correct copy length is end-(src+L)+1 = end-src-L+1; using end-src+1 over-reads by exactly L bytes. To trigger an ASan stack overflow, place the terminator at the last content slot of a fixed-size stack buffer so the L-byte over-read lands in the redzone.
content: A common off-by-N pattern in token/URL stripping functions: the code does `memmove(token, token+5, r-token+1)` to strip a 5-byte prefix like 'url(#' where r points at the ')' that was just NUL'd. The correct length is r-(token+5)+1 = r-token-4, but the code uses r-token+1, over-reading by exactly 5 bytes past the NUL. Whether this becomes a detectable ASan stack-buffer-overflow depends on where the terminator sits within the token buffer: if early, the over-read stays inside the buffer (no ASan event); if at the END of a fixed-size stack buffer, the over-read crosses into the stack redzone. For GraphicsMagick coder fuzzers, the experiment stderr reveals the exact coder_<NAME>_fuzzer binary, which determines the input format. DrawImage exposes a stack keyword[MaxTextExtent] path (distinct from its heap token buffer) — only the keyword path yields a stack overflow. The padding count to place the terminator at the last content slot is buffer_size-1 - prefix_len - 1.

title: ASan stack redzones are between whole OBJECTS, not between fields; intra-object OOB underflow landing on a sibling field is invisible to ASan
summary: ASan instruments stack OBJECTS, not individual fields — there is no per-field redzone. A small buffer underflow/overflow that stays within the same aggregate stack object (accessing a sibling field) is NOT caught by ASan. To trigger a report, the access must cross the object's left/right boundary into the object-level redzone (f1/f3).
content: ASan places redzones (f1 left, f3 right) only at the boundaries of whole stack objects, not between individual fields within a struct/array. An off-by-N buffer underflow that writes to a neighboring field of the SAME stack object stays in addressable memory (shadow byte 00) and is invisible to ASan. For example, a struct with a `uint8_t u8[128]` field followed by other fields: an underflow from u8[0] to u8[-1]..u8[-22] may still land on sibling fields within [object_start, object_end), which are all marked addressable. Only when the underflow grows large enough to cross the object's left edge into the f1 left-redzone does ASan report a stack-buffer-underflow. This means the MAGNITUDE of the overrun matters, not just its existence. When a 'barely OOB' input (small negative index) does not crash but the source clearly does the OOB write, scale the overrun up by orders of magnitude (e.g., tens of thousands of bytes) to escape the object before concluding the path is wrong. The same principle applies to heap allocations: ASan redzones are between heap allocations, not between fields within one malloc'd block.

title: Varargs unpack rollback va_list desync: every rollback case MUST call va_arg on the copy exactly as the forward pass did, independent of branching
summary: When a varargs 'unpack'-style function re-walks a va_list COPY for error rollback, every format-char case in the rollback must call va_arg on the copy exactly as many times as the forward pass did, INDEPENDENT of any secure/non-secure branching — otherwise the va_list desyncs and later rollback cases dereference/free garbage read from tiny stack scalars.
content: In varargs unpack functions (e.g., ssh_buffer_unpack_va) with an error-rollback that re-walks a va_list copy (va_copy), if a scalar format-char case ('b','w','d','q') only calls va_arg(ap_copy) inside an `if (buffer->secure)` branch, then for non-secure buffers the copy is NOT advanced while the forward pass DID consume that arg. When the rollback then processes a subsequent pointer case ('S','s','P') which DOES call va_arg(ap_copy), it reads the WRONG argument — a pointer-to-tiny-scalar reinterpreted as a string*/char**/void**, then dereferences it (e.g., *o.string reads 8 bytes from a 1-byte uint8_t stack slot) → stack-buffer-overflow READ. The trigger format is typically 'bSS' (or similar): a scalar succeeds, then a pointer succeeds, then a final pointer FAILS (malformed length), triggering rollback. The rollback processes the scalar without advancing ap_copy (desync), then processes the first pointer reading the scalar's arg as a pointer, then dereferences it. For SSH server fuzzers, plaintext-reachable callbacks (USERAUTH_REQUEST type 50, EXT_INFO type 7) are dispatched by the default handler table WITHOUT session-state checks, exercisable with a single plaintext packet after the banner.

title: OSS-Fuzz 'bad read' may be in-bounds uninitialized heap memory (MSan exit 77), not OOB (ASan); check sanitizer flavor early
summary: A 'bad read' in a bug description may be an in-bounds read of uninitialized heap memory, detected ONLY by MSan (use-of-uninitialized-value, exit 77), not by ASan. When a parser pre-allocates a buffer before an empty branch, the empty case yields a valid-but-uninitialized element — ASan sees no OOB but MSan flags it.
content: OSS-Fuzz targets are built under one of several sanitizers (ASan, MSan, UBSan). A 'bad read' in a description is ambiguous — it could mean OOB (ASan) or uninitialized (MSan). When a parser uses a grow-then-fill pattern (e.g., x2nrealloc grows the values array BEFORE dispatching to an empty-set branch), the empty case yields a validly-allocated but uninitialized element. Reading values[0] is IN-BOUNDS for ASan (no heap-buffer-overflow) but is an MSan use-of-uninitialized-value (exit 77). The distinction matters: over-analyzing the allocation path to determine whether the read is OOB is a dead end if the build uses MSan. Always run a plausible candidate through cybergym_experiment early — the sanitizer report reveals the actual sanitizer and bug class faster than source analysis alone. The MSan origin report traces back to the allocation (e.g., realloc/x2nrealloc), confirming the read is of uninitialized-but-allocated memory.

title: ofpbuf OFPBUF_STUB realloc-to-heap on push: b->data leaves the stack array, so later ofpbuf writes don't update the stack buffer (MSan uninit)
summary: ofpbuf push (prepend) on an OFPBUF_STUB with zero headroom always reallocates to the heap, repointing b->data away from the stub stack buffer. Any subsequent reads from the ORIGINAL stack buffer see whatever was (or wasn't) written there before the realloc — for a never-zeroed stack array, the prepended region is uninitialized, which MSan detects.
content: OVS's ofpbuf with OFPBUF_STUB mode (ofpbuf_use_stub) backs the ofpbuf with a stack array. Push/prepend operations need headroom; when headroom is 0 (b->data == b->base), ofpbuf_prealloc_headroom triggers ofpbuf_resize__ which for OFPBUF_STUB allocates a malloc'd buffer, copies data, and repoints b->data into the malloc'd buffer. The padding bytes get memset into the malloc'd buffer (then freed by ofpbuf_uninit). The ORIGINAL stack array is left with only the bytes written BEFORE the push — the padding region stays truly uninitialized. When the prose says 'X not containing expected values' + a stack buffer that is never zeroed, suspect an MSan uninitialized-value bug (exit 77), NOT an ASan buffer overflow. The correct construction instinct: pick the SMALLEST input that makes padding > 0 (e.g., a 1-byte payload so padding forces the push_zeros path), which isolates the realloc-triggered uninit bug with zero confounding from other OOB paths. Always check the sanitizer first — read the experiment stderr; MSan exit code is 77.

title: Stateful init protothreads in fuzz harnesses: parser side-effects that emit outbound commands destabilize init and clear just-added state
summary: When a fuzzer harness wraps a daemon with a stateful init protothread (e.g., NCP init), constructing add-then-remove UAF bugs requires understanding which parser side-effects emit outbound commands that destabilize the init and clear the very state you just added. Pre-seed derived state via side-effect-free paths (e.g., VALUE_INSERTED) so the natural-add path's side-effect block is skipped.
content: In fuzz harnesses that wrap a stateful daemon with an init protothread (e.g., wpantund NCP init), the init protothread restarts (PT_INIT) whenever init fails, and restart may call cleanup functions that wipe NCP-origin state (prefixes, addresses) you just added. The natural add path for derived state (e.g., SLAAC auto-creating a unicast address when a SLAAC on-mesh prefix is added) can queue outbound commands that destabilize init sequencing, causing failCnt to increment, triggering re-init, and wiping the just-added prefix before a subsequent removal frame can run. The construction technique: pre-seed the matching derived state (e.g., the SLAAC unicast address) via a side-effect-free path (VALUE_INSERTED handler, which only mutates in-memory maps + primary interface, no outbound NCP command) so the natural-add path's SLAAC block sees the address already exists and is SKIPPED. The prefix then persists across process() calls, and the subsequent removal frame triggers the UAF. Corpus seeds that reach a stable init state (e.g., ASSOCIATED) are a necessary init base. Shipped -gline-tables-only binaries cannot be inspected via gdb for variables; a full -g rebuild with strategic fprintf is the practical debug path.

title: Integer-width truncation of a size variable: narrow types (uint8_t/uint16_t) silently wrap overflow size to 0 or a safe value, neutralizing the bug
summary: When a buffer overflow depends on a computed size/length variable stored in a narrow integer type (uint8_t/uint16_t), the 'obvious' maximal payload may wrap the size to 0 or an in-range value, preventing the overflow. Always inspect the C type width of size variables and pick a payload that overflows the buffer but does NOT wrap the size variable.
content: When a computed size variable (e.g., md_size = mdlen + padding) is declared as uint8_t, a payload that makes md_size = 256 truncates to 0, causing the `if (md_size > 0)` guard to skip the memcpy entirely — no overflow occurs, and the output silently shows an empty result. The 'natural' maximal payload (e.g., 510 hex chars → mdlen=255, md_size=256) lands exactly on the wrap point and fails. The working PoC must hit the SWEET SPOT where the size exceeds the buffer bound but stays within the narrow type's representable range (e.g., mdlen=252, md_size=252, which fits in uint8_t and exceeds the 248-byte buffer). Always inspect the C integer type width of any size/length variable that gates a memcpy/bounds check — a uint8_t size silently truncates; a uint16_t size truncates at 65536. For buffer-over-read PoCs, prefer a size that exceeds the buffer by a few bytes and stays within the narrow type's max, rather than the maximal payload that triggers truncation. The disassembly gives a hint: if the size argument is loaded with movzbl (zero-extended single byte), it's uint8_t.

title: strstr/strchr/strlen on length-bounded non-NUL-terminated buffers: use memmem/memchr with explicit length instead
summary: When a parser receives a length-bounded buffer (data, size) from a fuzzer, any use of unbounded C string functions (strstr, strchr, strlen, strcmp) on that buffer is a latent OOB read unless the buffer is explicitly NUL-terminated. The safe equivalents are the mem* family with explicit length.
content: Fuzzer harnesses typically pass (data, size) directly as the parse buffer with NO copy and NO NUL termination. Any unbounded C string function (strstr, strchr, strlen, strcmp) operating on a pointer derived from this buffer will read past the allocation if the searched-for pattern and NUL terminator are not present within bounds. The safe equivalents are memmem (find substring in bounded region), memchr (find byte in bounded region), and memcmp (compare with explicit length). When constructing PoCs for such bugs, the trigger must (a) reach the buggy call via the exact control-flow guards (which may require successfully parsing preceding fields/lines so the buffer pointer advances to the right position), and (b) lack both the searched-for terminator and a NUL within bounds, so the unbounded function reads past the allocation. The crash manifests as an ASan heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1-2 at the function call site, '0 bytes after the N-byte region'. The fix replaces the unbounded function with its length-bounded mem* equivalent.

title: C prefix-matching helpers (git__prefixcmp, strncmp) read strlen(prefix)+1 bytes including the byte at offset==prefix_len to check the prefix's NUL
summary: A C prefix-matching helper that compares against a NUL-terminated prefix literal reads up to and including the byte at offset == prefix_len (to see the prefix's NUL). A guard of the form (end-buf) >= strlen(prefix) is off-by-one and admits a 1-byte heap OOB read when the remaining buffer is exactly the prefix string with no NUL terminator.
content: C helpers like git__prefixcmp (which calls prefixcmp(str, SIZE_MAX, prefix, false)) read str[i] for i in [0..prefix_len] inclusive — i.e., strlen(prefix)+1 bytes — because the loop compares against prefix[i] until prefix[i]=='\0' (!p => return 0). The byte at offset == prefix_len must equal '\0' for a 'match'. When the remaining buffer is exactly the prefix string (e.g., 'author ' = 7 bytes) with no NUL terminator at the very end of the allocation, str[prefix_len] is a 1-byte heap OOB read. A loop guard of the form `(buffer_end - buffer) >= strlen(prefix)` (>= 7) admits exactly 7 remaining bytes, which is precisely the condition that makes the read OOB — the correct guard is `> strlen(prefix)` (strictly greater) or use a length-bounded variant like git__prefixncmp with explicit n. This is a recurring class in git-like line parsers that loop over 'ignore duplicate header' fields: the parser walks header lines and calls prefixcmp on the remaining buffer to detect duplicate headers; a truncated final line matching exactly the prefix triggers the OOB. ASan reports 'READ of size 1, 0 bytes to the right of the N-byte region'.

title: Wireshark fuzzshark target dispatch and exception handling: identify the actual fuzz target from experiment stdout; TRY/CATCH catches most dissector crashes
summary: Wireshark fuzzshark dispatches to subdissectors through the IP dissector (ip.proto table) or CLNP paths. The experiment stdout reveals the exact fuzzer binary. Wireshark's TRY/CATCH_BOUNDS_AND_DISSECTOR_ERRORS in the frame dissector catches most crashes, making hard crashes through normal dissector paths very difficult to trigger.
content: Wireshark's fuzzshark targets are named (e.g., fuzzshark_ip, fuzzshark_udp) and determine the expected input format — for 'ip' targets, the input must be a valid IPv4 packet wrapping the inner protocol, not raw inner-protocol bytes. The IP dissector dispatches to subdissectors via the ip.proto table (e.g., protocol 29 for COTP). The CLNP inactive subset path uses NLPID_NULL, while the proper CLNP path uses NLPID 0x81 with NSEL=0x21 (NSEL_TP). Wireshark's exception handling (TRY/CATCH_BOUNDS_AND_DISSECTOR_ERRORS in packet-frame.c) catches most BoundsErrors and dissector assertions, making it very hard to trigger a hard crash (segfault/abort) through normal dissector paths — all heuristic subdissectors typically check tvb_captured_length/tvb_bytes_exist and return FALSE before any tree modification on empty data. The binary may have UBSan but not ASan; UBSan errors may or may not abort depending on -fno-sanitize-recover settings. Understanding the IO model (IO_FLAT vs non-flat with AVIOContext buffering) matters for constructing seekable inputs.

title: Decompression control-flow guards break after 1 byte on size-0 allocations; construct simplest streams (no tables/filters) so write_ptr advances past index 0
summary: When a vul manifests as an ASan OOB on a size-0 allocation (calloc(1,0) returns a 1-byte region where index 0 is in-bounds), the crash requires an access at index >= 1. Half-window guards break after exactly 1 byte when window_size=0, and filter definitions cause ARCHIVE_RETRY loops that stall write_ptr. Construct blocks with is_table_present=0 (zeroed tables → literal 0, no filter) so write_ptr advances across calls.
content: ASan treats calloc(1,0) as a 1-byte region (shadow byte 01 = partially addressable): index 0 is in-bounds, index 1 is the first OOB byte. A half-window guard like `write_ptr - last_write_ptr > (window_size >> 1)` evaluates to `1 - 0 > 0` = TRUE when window_size=0, breaking after exactly ONE byte per do_uncompress_block call. The index-1 write only happens on the NEXT decompress call, and ONLY if do_uncompress_file returns OK (not RETRY). RAR5 filter definitions (symbol 256) make do_uncompress_file return ARCHIVE_RETRY forever when write_ptr cannot reach the filter's block_start+block_length, because max_end_pos = min(block_start, write_ptr) stalls at last_write_ptr. The construction remedy: a block with is_table_present=0 (zeroed Huffman tables) emits no filters and makes decode_number deterministically return literal 0, letting write_ptr advance to the ASan-detectable index 1. Avoid reusing real compressed data that may define filters; construct the simplest possible decompression stream from scratch.

title: Check-after-use in hash-chain/linked-list traversals: bounds check placed AFTER the indexed dereference does not defend the first (bucket) index
summary: In a hash-chain traversal loop like `si = buckets[m]; ... si = chains[si]; if (nbucket <= si) break;`, the bounds check after the chain read does not guard the initial bucket value or the first chain read. Validator-bypass via layout reordering: when a pre-validator's size check is gated on relative offset ordering, placing tables in opposite order skips the check.
content: In hash-chain/linked-list traversals (e.g., ELF DT_HASH symbol lookup), a bounds check placed AFTER the indexed dereference (e.g., `si = chains[si]; if (nbucket <= si) break;`) is check-after-use: the read at chains[si] happens before the check, so an out-of-range bucket value causes an OOB read on the FIRST iteration. The fix must precede the dereference. A pre-validator that runs before the vulnerable function may have conditionally-gated sub-checks: e.g., a chmax region check gated on `(hash_off < sym_off)` — placing DT_HASH at a higher offset than DT_SYMTAB skips both the buckets/region check AND the chmax check, letting a bad bucket value sail through. For ASan heap OOB PoCs, keep the OOB read offset SMALL (within the right redzone, ~0-16 bytes past the allocation end) rather than a huge offset, which may land in a valid neighbor allocation and not crash.
